questions.question: What does RGB-D mean, and what does each image provide?
questions.author: /root/workflow_worker
questions.short_answer: RGB-D means red, green and blue colour plus depth. The colour image tells the detector where a body landmark appears. The aligned depth image supplies its metric depth. Together with the camera calibration, they give a 3D position.
questions.supporting_detail: RGB records appearance in red, green and blue channels. The D435 estimates depth by stereo triangulation with infrared texture assistance. This pipeline discards MediaPipe's appearance-derived depth and samples the aligned sensor depth at each landmark pixel.
questions.sources: Sections 2.3, D.1-D.3; printed 14, D1-D3; PDF 28, 145-147.
questions.limits: Depth can belong to the cube or desk in front of the body. A metric sample is still an imperfect surface measurement.

questions.question: What is the difference between tracking and reconstruction here?
questions.author: /root/workflow_worker
questions.short_answer: Tracking extracts body landmarks and object poses from successive images. Reconstruction uses those measurements, the body geometry and the scene calibration to place an avatar and cube in a shared 3 D scene.
questions.supporting_detail: The detector supplies eight body points; the kinematic solve turns them into a root pose and arm angles. Unity composes those rotations on the rig. When observations fail, reconstruction may use constraints or hold earlier values, so rendered motion is not always newly observed motion.
questions.sources: Abstract; Chapter 3 opening; Section 6.3; printed iii-iv, 21, 74-75; PDF 3-4, 35, 88-89.
questions.limits: A convincing replay does not establish anatomical accuracy.
questions.supporting_slide: Main slides 17, 42. 17 Torso frame; 42 Rig application

questions.question: How do position, orientation and six degrees of freedom differ?
questions.author: /root/workflow_worker
questions.short_answer: Position says where a point is. Orientation says how a frame is turned. A rigid object's pose contains three translation coordinates and three rotational degrees of freedom; a wrist landmark alone supplies only position.
questions.supporting_detail: A marker supplies four known corners, allowing the solver to estimate its frame's rotation and translation. Body landmarks are points without attached orientations. The model derives segment frames from their geometry, but this does not make every anatomical rotation observable.
questions.sources: Chapter 3 opening; Sections 2.2.1, E.2; printed 21, 11-12, E3-E4; PDF 35, 25-26, 151-152.
questions.limits: Six degrees of freedom do not mean six independent reliable measurements; a planar marker can admit two competing poses.
questions.supporting_slide: Main slides 15, 21. 15 Camera and Camera-prime; 21 Object pose

questions.question: What are camera, world and local frames?
questions.author: /root/workflow_worker
questions.short_answer: A frame is an origin and three axes used to describe coordinates. The camera frame starts at the colour camera. The world frame is fixed to the desk marker. A local frame moves with a body segment or the object.
questions.supporting_detail: The raw camera has x right, y down and z forward. Camera-prime flips y and shares the optical origin. The Unity convention retains the desk origin; gravity alignment and floor placement produce Scene. Body-segment frames describe rotations along the arm chain.
questions.limits: Changing coordinates does not change the physical motion. Axis flips and swaps reverse handedness and must not be treated as proper rotations.
questions.supporting_slide: Main slides 15, 21, 41. 15 Camera and Camera-prime; 21 Object pose; 41 Mapping into Scene

questions.question: How is calibration different from filtering?
questions.author: /root/workflow_worker
questions.short_answer: Calibration establishes the camera geometry, scene frames and body lengths used to interpret measurements. Filtering reduces spikes and rapid variation in the measurements over time. Smoother data can still have calibration bias.
questions.supporting_detail: Factory intrinsics map pixels and depth into camera coordinates. The first ten static-marker detections establish frozen scene anchors. Temporal filtering then despikes, bridges short interior gaps and smooths valid runs. The frozen anchor avoids repeated anchor wobble but can preserve an initial bias.
questions.limits: Filtering does not prove or repair an incorrect metric scale or gravity reference.
questions.supporting_slide: Main slides 10-12; Hidden slides 96-98. Use the stated comparison references and conditions. Later demonstrations, literature and benchmarks are supplementary; they do not replace final-thesis evidence.

questions.question: What are forward and inverse kinematics in this project?
questions.author: /root/workflow_worker
questions.short_answer: Forward kinematics reconstructs the arm from joint rotations and link geometry. Inverse kinematics finds a compatible configuration from observed endpoints. The shoulder and wrist leave a circle of possible elbows only when their separation is strictly between the folded and fully extended limits.
questions.supporting_detail: With link lengths L1 and L2 and shoulder-to-wrist distance r, a nondegenerate circle requires abs(L1-L2) < r < L1+L2. For separated endpoints at either boundary, the spheres touch at one point. Outside reach they have no exact intersection; coincident endpoints are another degenerate case. For a circle, direction memory selects a point before the rotations are composed for display.
questions.sources: Sections 5.5, 6.3, H.1; printed 58-59, 74-75, H1; PDF 72-73, 88-89, 162; equation (5.8), PDF 73; v1/kinematics/occlusion_ext.py:334-374.
questions.limits: The endpoints and remembered direction do not generally determine the true hidden elbow. Not every reachable configuration yields a circle.
questions.supporting_slide: Main slides 29, 31; Hidden slides 73, 78. 29 Two segment-length constraints; 31 Deriving the elbow circle; 73 Two-link reconstruction; 78 Solver verification

questions.question: What do measured, held and constrained outputs mean?
questions.author: /root/workflow_worker
questions.short_answer: Measured means the solve uses accepted current observations. Held means the required geometry is unavailable and the joint group keeps its last solved value. Constrained means the solve uses a repaired point or recovery constraint.
questions.supporting_detail: These states describe the evidence behind an output, rather than its accuracy. Hip or shoulder preparation can make the root constrained as well as the arms. A successfully solved group consuming a repaired point loses its live bit; a group that cannot be solved is held.
questions.sources: Abstract; Appendix G.4; printed iii-iv, G3; PDF 3-4, 161.
questions.limits: Measured does not mean independently validated. Smooth held or constrained output can be wrong.
questions.supporting_slide: Main slides 18-19, 23. 18 Shoulder swing; 19 Shoulder twist; 23 Output states

questions.question: What is ground truth, and what references do your errors use?
questions.author: /root/workflow_worker
questions.short_answer: Ground truth is an independently known reference for the quantity being estimated. Here the exact injected synthetic trajectories are known by construction. The recording comparisons use more limited references: tape lengths, accepted raw landmarks, manual wrist labels and the unmasked reconstruction. Each supports a different claim.
questions.supporting_detail: Tape lengths test endpoint separation, not the complete path in world coordinates. Raw landmark comparisons test agreement with the sensor input. Synthetic removal compares recovery with the valid unmasked model, and natural occlusion compares with manual wrist labels. None is independent full-body anatomical ground truth.

questions.question: How are accuracy and precision different?
questions.author: /root/workflow_worker
questions.short_answer: Accuracy concerns agreement with the true quantity; precision concerns agreement between repeated measurements under stated conditions. A stable estimate can be consistently biased. I report errors against each named reference rather than calling small scatter proof of accuracy.
questions.supporting_detail: The thesis uses physical length errors and positional differences against stated references. Marker corners repeatedly landing on whole pixels can look stable because of quantization. The metrology definition also treats accuracy as a concept, not a numerical quantity with its own unit.
questions.sources: Section 7.1, E.1; printed 85, E2; PDF 99, 150; [JCGM VIM accuracy](https://jcgm.bipm.org/vim/en/2.13.html), [precision](https://jcgm.bipm.org/vim/en/2.15.html), read 2026-09-29.
questions.limits: Trajectory scatter along a moving task is not automatically a repeatability experiment.
questions.supporting_slide: Main slides 8, 21. 8 Calibration; 21 Object pose

questions.question: How do throughput and latency differ in your real-time claim?
questions.author: /root/workflow_worker
questions.short_answer: Throughput is how many frames the system processes per second. Latency is how long an individual frame takes to reach the displayed result. Replay kept up at about 29 frames per second, but sensor-to-screen latency was not measured.
questions.supporting_detail: The thesis separates the configured two-frame buffering delay, motion-dependent filter lag and the five-frame alignment of two angle series. The branch processing times fit the frame budget on the stated workstation. Those facts do not measure or bound the complete sensor-to-screen delay.
questions.sources: Sections 8.4-8.5; printed 114-115; PDF 128-129.
questions.limits: The later transport-package benchmark is a separate presentation experiment, not a thesis end-to-end latency measurement.

questions.question: Why use one camera, and what can it never directly see?
questions.author: /root/workflow_worker
questions.short_answer: One RGB-D camera gives colour and metric depth without a camera array or sensors attached to the subject. It still has one viewpoint. A wrist hidden behind the object has no direct visible-surface depth observation.
questions.supporting_detail: The detector can predict a landmark even when it is hidden. Alignment puts colour and depth on a shared ray, but the returned depth belongs to the visible surface. The recovery layer therefore uses remembered geometry and object constraints when observations fail.

questions.question: Why combine body landmarks with object markers?
questions.author: /root/workflow_worker
questions.short_answer: The landmarks locate the person. The markers establish a fixed scene frame and measure the object pose. If the hand is holding the cube and its wrist measurement fails, the object pose supplies another geometric constraint.
questions.supporting_detail: The held hand uses a learned hand-to-object offset, carried by the current object pose; the arm still depends on calibrated lengths and direction memory. Desk and object markers are printed 45 mm squares. The pinned detector-size correction places all thesis translations on that settled 45 mm scale.

questions.question: Why can you locate the wrist without knowing its full orientation?
questions.author: /root/workflow_worker
questions.short_answer: A wrist landmark is one point. It does not show how the hand rotates around the forearm. The model can reconstruct an arm ending at that point without claiming a measured wrist orientation.
questions.supporting_detail: Segment geometry gives the directions between landmarks and supports the solved arm angles. Rotating the hand around an unchanged wrist point does not change those point coordinates. The thesis explicitly treats the wrist as a tracked point.

questions.question: How do offline and causal processing differ?
questions.author: /root/workflow_worker
questions.short_answer: Offline processing can read later frames. Causal processing uses only samples already received. Forward-backward filtering and interior-gap interpolation use future observations, so the real-time structure needs different operations.
questions.supporting_detail: A trailing despiker and One Euro filter replace the centred offline stages. The merger can interpolate between samples already in its buffer by displaying an older time. A replay using this causal structure is different from retrospective offline smoothing.
questions.limits: Causality does not mean zero lag. A complete live-camera session was not validated.
questions.supporting_slide: Main slides 57; Hidden slides 101, 103. 57 One Euro adaptive smoothing; 101 One Euro filtering; 103 Why One Euro in real time Later demonstrations, literature and benchmarks are supplementary; they do not replace final-thesis evidence.

questions.question: How is the printed marker size carried consistently into the measurements?

questions.question: Why average ten initial detections and then freeze the anchors?
questions.author: /root/worker_qa_methods
questions.short_answer: Averaging reduces initial noise, and freezing prevents later marker jitter from moving the whole scene. Ten detections is the design window used here; I do not have a sensitivity study that establishes it as optimal.
questions.supporting_detail: Translation uses a mean. Rotation uses an element-wise mean followed by SVD projection onto a proper rotation. Small changes at printed precision are not a statistical spread estimate. Freezing also freezes initial bias, and movement of the camera or anchors afterwards invalidates the calibration.

questions.question: How can a 2.9 cm spike be rejected with a 2 cm Hampel floor?
questions.author: /root/worker_qa_methods
questions.short_answer: The 2 cm floor is on the rejection threshold. The test rejects a residual above the larger of 2 cm and three times the robust scale, so a 2.9 cm residual can be rejected.
questions.supporting_detail: Code computes threshold=max(abs_floor, k*1.4826*MAD), with k=3 and abs_floor=0.02 m. MAD is a centred rolling median of each sample's residual from its own centred rolling median, rather than all deviations from one common window median. The rejected point becomes missing before gap interpolation.

questions.limits: Implementation verified.

questions.question: What justifies fourth-order Butterworth smoothing at 3 Hz, and what does the double pass cost?
questions.author: /root/worker_qa_methods
questions.short_answer: It is the offline design used to reduce jitter in this slow task. Forward and backward filtering cancels phase delay but increases attenuation near the cutoff. The thesis does not establish the cutoff from a measured motion spectrum.

It is supplementary evidence, not a result originally reported by V9, and deviation from a measured trace is not error against independent truth.
